title: Three Banal Scripts

source.quote: The basic training of life includes a systematic attack on three primary human potentials: the potential for intimacy ... the potential for awareness ... and the potential for spontaneity .... I have called the end result of this three-part basic training Lovelessness, Mindlessness, and Joylessness.

setting: Thursday. Marcus is describing his week at dinner. Later that same week, Zara gets home from work.

L1.line: Yeah, it's been a brutal week - client fires, picked up Jess from school twice because Priya's traveling, then I stayed up redoing the Hendricks deck after everyone else bailed. It's fine though, I'm fine.
cues: laughs it off between each item
describes himself as 'fine' through a stifled yawn and red eyes
L1.question: Quick primer: Steiner names three everyday, undramatic scripts - Lovelessness, Mindlessness, Joylessness - and, separately, a 'sex-role script': boys commonly trained to switch off their own needs and feelings while calmly handling everything, girls trained the opposite way. Which pattern best names what's going on with Marcus?

options.text: He's just got a strong work ethic - this isn't script.
options.feedback: 'Just' is doing a lot of work in that sentence. What reads as personality - never asking, never resting, always fine - is exactly the shape Steiner and Wyckoff describe being trained into boys: it doesn't feel like a decision because it was made so early and reinforced so often.

options.text: He's in the Be Strong driver, nothing more.
options.feedback: Be Strong is present in the half-second tells - the flat 'I'm fine,' the no-ask for help - but that's the moment-to-moment behavior. Marcus's whole week is organized around something bigger than one driver flashing on and off.

options.text: This is the male sex-role script Steiner and Wyckoff describe: Adult built up for 'handling business,' Nurturing Parent switched on only for others, Natural Child almost entirely shut down.
options.feedback: Right. Notice what's missing from his whole account: anything he felt, wanted, or needed. That's not an accident of the story - it's the training working exactly as designed.

He may well be stroke-starved too, but that's a plausible side effect, not what this particular pattern is naming. The training here is about which ego states he's allowed to use at all, not just a shortage of strokes.

L1.lesson: Steiner and Wyckoff's sex-role analysis is structural, not a personality judgment: boys are trained to over-build Adult and Nurturing-Parent-for-others while leaving their own Natural Child almost entirely offline. It looks like a personality - that's the whole point of calling it a script.

L2.intro: Zara gets home. Across one evening, the Pig Parent in her head narrates three ordinary moments - and she decides, each time, whether to obey it.

beats.line: Don't let that in. He's just saying it because he wants something.
cues: her partner just said 'you look nice today'
her shoulders tighten before she's even answered

options.outcome: He shrugs, a little puzzled. The moment passes with the stroke uncollected.
options.lesson: This obeys the Pig Parent's Stroke Economy rule - don't take in a stroke you haven't 'earned' - so cleanly it doesn't even feel like a rule being followed.

options.text: "Thank you - that's really nice to hear."
options.outcome: Something in her actually relaxes. 'Oh - thank you,' she says again, meaning it the second time.
options.lesson: Breaking the Stroke Economy isn't complicated: it's letting a stroke land instead of deflecting it. Steiner's whole therapy for Lovelessness is teaching people to do exactly this, on purpose.

options.text: "You're just saying that because you want something."
options.outcome: He looks hurt. 'I just meant you look nice.' A small fight starts out of nowhere.
options.lesson: Rejecting a stroke before it can be 'taken away' does the same job as discounting it quietly - same rule, enforced louder.

options.text: "Oh, this old thing? I look terrible, actually."
options.outcome: He reassures her again. She doesn't quite believe it the second time either.
options.lesson: Fishing for more strokes looks like the opposite of refusing them, but it runs on the same scarcity belief - that strokes have to be earned or extracted, never simply received.

beats.line: Don't make a scene. You probably read it wrong anyway.
cues: Zara spots a number that doesn't add up on the budget slide
her boss is already moving confidently to the next point

options.text: (Say nothing. Later, wonder if she imagined it.)
options.outcome: The deck goes out with the error in it. Nobody mentions it until a client does, two weeks later.
options.lesson: This is Mindlessness exactly as Steiner names it - not failing to notice, but discounting what she did notice. The data was there; she overrode it.

options.text: "I think line four might be off - can we check it together?"
options.outcome: They check. She's right. Her boss says 'good catch' and actually means it.
options.lesson: Countering Mindlessness isn't about being certain - it's about not discounting the Adult data you already have, stated as something checkable instead of swallowed as a private doubt.

options.outcome: She's right, but the room reads it as an outburst, and the correction gets lost in the reaction to her tone.
options.lesson: Right content delivered as an eruption still gets discounted - by other people this time, which teaches the same lesson about staying quiet next time.

options.text: "You're probably right, I just wasn't paying attention." (though she was)
options.outcome: The error ships. She gets a quiet compliment afterward for being easy to work with.
options.lesson: Steiner's point about lying applies here too - lying to herself about what she noticed gets socially rewarded, which is exactly why it's so hard to stop doing.

beats.line: You've earned this. Numb out - you don't need to feel anything else today.
cues: she's alone in the kitchen, still in her coat
hand already reaching for the cabinet where the wine lives
hasn't noticed yet that her shoulders are up by her ears

options.outcome: She's asleep on the couch by nine, still in her coat, and wakes at midnight just as tense as she started.
options.lesson: Reaching for the substance before noticing the body is the exact move Steiner is naming - it skips the sensation instead of answering it, so the tension is still there underneath.

options.text: (Pause. Notice her shoulders. Breathe. Then decide.)
options.outcome: She notices she's actually hungrier than tense. She makes dinner. The wine stays in the cabinet, and that's fine too.
options.lesson: The counter-move isn't willpower or abstinence - it's reconnecting to what the body is actually saying before acting on autopilot. Steiner calls this Centering.

options.text: (Keep working past dinner, to 'earn' rest later.)
options.outcome: She finishes the task at 11pm, numb, and feels no satisfaction even though the work is good.
options.lesson: Joylessness isn't only substances - any reliable way of not feeling the body counts, overwork included.

options.outcome: She feels genuinely lighter after the call. She still never actually checks in with her own body tonight.
options.lesson: Connecting with another person is good, and it's real - and it's not the same move as reconnecting with her own sensation. The two get confused because both bring relief.

echo.setting: A week later. Zara's manager tells her, in front of the team, that the client loved her proposal.
echo.line: The Pig Parent is already loading: 'Don't let that in, they're just being nice.' This time she catches it before she answers.
echo.shape: same take-it-in-or-deflect choice as L2's first beat
